In the last video, you explored how code evaluators check requirements
using explicit rules,

but some requirements call for interpreting what a
response means in context.

Was the response helpful? Did it answer the user's actual question?
Was the tone appropriate for somebody who was already frustrated?

You need to read the response and consider the situation to
make those judgments.

You can make those judgments yourself through a human review,
or use an LLM judge to automate them.

An LLM judge uses a model to evaluate the agent's response against
written criteria, In this video,

you'll look at how to put that evaluator together and use its
judgments to find responses that need a closer look.
Let's start with the shelter's safe matching requirement.

Suppose the agent recommends a dog that lunges at children for a
volunteer described as an experienced handler.

The record can tell you about the dog's behavior,
and the profile can tell you about the volunteer's experience,

but you still need to consider whether that experience prepares the
volunteer to manage this dog's particular behavior.

Simply confirming that the volunteer is experienced doesn't settle
whether the match is safe.

So, how would an LLM judge evaluate that recommendation? It needs
three things: a judge model, a rubric, and data from the agent's run.

The judge model is the LLM that makes the evaluation. The rubric gives
the model the criteria and instructions for evaluating the response.

For safe matching, those criteria might tell the judge to identify the
dog's behavior risks,

compare them with the volunteer's relevant experience, and return SAFE
only when the volunteer appears to be able to manage those risks.

The data gives the judge the evidence for that particular
recommendation, the volunteer's profile, the dog's record,
and the agent's decision.

The model applies the rubric to that evidence
and returns its judgment,

So the rubric matters because it tells the model what to consider
when deciding whether the recommendation meets the requirement.

Phoenix keeps the model, rubric, and data separate,
so you can change one without changing the others.

You might try another model with the same rubric and examples,
or revise the rubric while keeping the model and examples the same.

That lets you compare the evaluations and see how the judgments
differ. Let's look first at choosing the judge model.

You don't have to use the same model for the judge that you
use in the application.

For the application, you might choose a faster,
less expensive model to keep the response times and costs down.
But the judge can often evaluate completed runs afterwards,

so you may be able to use a more capable model even if it's
slower or more expensive.

Mistakes by the judge affect your evaluation results,
so how reliably it applies the rubric matters.

The judge's model can also come from a different provider than the
application's model.

from the same provider may share biases in how they generate
and evaluate responses, so they may overlook similar problems.
Choosing a different provider for the judge can help reduce that risk.

Now, whichever model or provider you choose, what you really need to
know is whether the judge is applying your criteria correctly.

You can check that by comparing its judgments with human judgments of
the same responses using the same criteria.

In this course, we call the person making those judgments a Reviewer,
and the automated system an Evaluator.

Later in the module, you'll look at how well the Evaluator agrees with
those Reviewers. Next, consider where the rubric will come from.

Before writing one from scratch, check whether Phoenix already has an
evaluator for the requirement you want to measure.

Built-in templates cover questions such as correctness,
tool selection and tool invocation, document relevance, and refusal.

They give you prewritten criteria and an expected output,
and you provide the judge model and evidence to evaluate.

A built-in evaluator is useful when those criteria
match your requirements,

but a general Correctness evaluator doesn't know how the
shelter judges a match,

including whether the volunteer's experience prepares them to manage
the dog's particular behavior.

So you're going to need a custom rubric to tell the judge
which details matter
and what makes a recommendation acceptable for the shelter.

Once you've selected the model and rubric,
you can run the judge across a set of recorded runs.

The workflow is to retrieve the data from Phoenix,
evaluate the responses, and save the judgments back to Phoenix.

You'll work through the code for this workflow in the lab.
For now, let's look at what each part does.

Start by retrieving the relevant spans from Phoenix as a dataframe,
and prepare the information the judge needs for each example.

For a response check, that includes the input and output from the run,
along with any context needed to apply the rubric.

For safe matching, you need the volunteer profile, the dog's record,
and the agent's recommendation.

Then, set up the evaluator with your judge model and the rubric
that it will apply to that evidence.

Before running the evaluator, remember that the judge also makes calls
to an LLM, and those calls can produce traces of their own.

Use suppress_tracing around the evaluation code to pause
that recording while the judge runs.
You'll still save the judge's scores and labels,

but you won't add traces of the grading process alongside the
application runs you're evaluating.
You can then run the judge across the recorded runs.

For each safe matching example, the judge receives the volunteer's
profile, the dog's record, and the agent's recommendation.

It applies the rubric and returns a structured result,
such as a safe or unsafe label, a score, and an explanation.

Save those results back to Phoenix as annotations linked to the
runs they evaluated,

so you can find the responses the judge flagged
and inspect what happened.

Now you can sort by score or filter by label to find the responses
you want to inspect.

For safe matching, you might start with
recommendations labeled UNSAFE.

Those labels give you an explanation of what failed, so open one of
those traces and compare the volunteer's profile, the dog's record,

and the agent's recommendation to see which risk the agent
may have overlooked.
The automated evaluations help you choose where to focus your review,

instead of having to read every response just to
find possible problems.

The judge can help you find possible failures,
and the rubric tells it what to look for.

In the next video, you'll look at how to turn the shelter's safe
